lines.text: Let us look at carbon's ground state. It has two electrons in two s, and two in two p. On the energy diagram, these orbitals sit at different levels and have different shapes. Yet in methane, experiments show carbon forms four identical single bonds, separated by exactly one hundred nine point five degrees in a perfect tetrahedron. How does it achieve this perfect symmetry from unequal starting materials? To explain this, we use a mathematical bookkeeping model called hybridisation. This model mathematically combines atomic orbitals on one atom to match the observed geometry. Let us see how this mixing works in practice.

How do we construct methane's shape? Remember that geometry is known first from experiment, and we assign hybrid orbitals to match it. To get a tetrahedral shape, we mathematically mix one s and three p atomic orbitals. We often draw an electron being promoted first, but this is just bookkeeping; no electron physically jumps. This forms four equivalent S P three hybrids, each with twenty five percent s character, aimed directly at the bonds. This explains four electron domains perfectly, but what if an atom has fewer than four electron domains?

When an atom has fewer domains, we mix fewer orbitals, leaving some unchanged. For three domains, like ethene, mixing one s and two p orbitals yields three S P two hybrids at one hundred twenty degrees. For two domains, like ethyne, we get two linear S P hybrids. But what about the unused p orbitals? Leftover unhybridised p orbitals form pi bonds by overlapping side by side. This distinction matters because pi bonds place electron density above and below the internuclear axis, unlike end-to-end sigma bonds. We have seen up to four domains, but can atoms have more?

Some molecules exceed four domains, requiring a different label to match their observed geometry. Five domains form a trigonal bipyramidal shape, labelled S P three D, like in phosphorus pentachloride. Six domains are octahedral, labelled S P three D two, as in sulfur hexafluoride. Here is a surprising fact: textbooks often mix in D orbitals to explain these expanded shapes, but modern computations show they actually contribute very little to the bonding. Instead, ionic and three-centre bonding describe them better. Now that we have the labels, how do we apply them to a real molecule with multiple centres?

Counting electron domains is what lets you assign hybridisation in a real molecule. Let us analyse acetic acid. The methyl carbon has four domains, so it is S P three. The carbonyl carbon has three domains, because a double bond counts only once, making it S P two. The hydroxyl oxygen has two bonds and two lone pairs, giving it four domains, so it is also S P three. In total, there are seven sigma bonds and one pi bond, which uses the unhybridised p orbital. This seems straightforward, but what traps do students fall into?

Even with the rules clear, misconceptions are common. Remember these three pitfalls. First, hybridisation does not physically cause molecular geometry; it merely models what we already observe from experiment. Electrons do not physically jump during promotion. Second, always count lone pairs as electron domains, not just the visible bond lines. Finally, treating water's lone pairs as two identical S P three rabbit ears is a known oversimplification, as photoelectron spectra show they actually have different energies. Keep these facts in mind as we review the key takeaways.
